analysis.one_liner: Blocks major federal regulations from taking effect unless Congress affirmatively votes to approve them.
analysis.headline: The REINS Act, which would have required Congress to vote before any major federal rule could take effect, was referred to committee, received hearings, and never came to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The REINS Act would have flipped how federal regulations work. Today, agencies can issue major rules — those affecting the economy by $100 million or more — unless Congress affirmatively votes to stop them. Under this bill, the opposite would be true: no major rule could take effect unless both chambers of Congress passed, and the president signed, a resolution approving it within 70 days. If Congress did nothing, the rule would simply die. An emergency 90-day window would exist for rules needed for imminent health or safety threats, criminal enforcement, or national security. The bill sat in the Senate Homeland Security committee, got two hearings, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing costly federal regulation — pollution limits, workplace safety standards, financial rules, consumer protections — would gain a powerful tool: they would no longer need to persuade Congress to repeal a rule, only to block one vote from ever happening. Wealthy households and large companies that bear most compliance costs would gain the most in absolute terms. Ordinary people would gain only if the rules being blocked were, on net, worse than useless; the bill also gives Congress (and thus voters) an on-the-record vote on every major regulation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated industries and their trade groups

how_it_helps.text: It restores a measure of legislative accountability: rules costing $100 million or more a year could not take effect unless both chambers affirmatively approved them by law, ending the practice in which agencies finalize major rules that no member of Congress ever votes on

It requires agencies to submit cost-benefit analyses and other supporting materials to Congress and the Comptroller General, and gives Congress fast-tracked procedures to force an up-or-down vote within roughly 70 days

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost when protective rules die by default: dirtier air and water, weaker workplace and product safety, and less consumer and financial oversight. Congress would also take on a workload it could not realistically sustain, meaning many needed rules would lapse regardless of their merits.

drawbacks.text: Any rule affecting more than $100 million a year would need a new law to take effect, and Congress has historically been unable to pass even budgets on time, so many public protections would lapse by default
Industry would only need to block one vote to kill a rule, while supporters of the rule would need to win approval in both chambers and get a president's signature — a heavily asymmetric process
The bill provides no deadline-driven path to approve rules that both parties want, so routine rules protecting air, water, workplaces, and consumers would routinely expire

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real constitutional accountability — no major rule would take effect without an affirmative act of Congress, a genuine check on unaccountable executive lawmaking. But the cost side is severe: with a divided, slow-moving Congress, many protective rules would simply die in the 70-day window, including safety, health, and consumer standards that benefit millions. A fast-tracked approval process for blocking rules (but not for passing them) tilts the design toward deregulation. Weighing these honestly, the accountability gain comes bundled with a high risk of losing protections that are cheaper and more effective to enforce through expert agencies than through 535 votes each.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Homeland Security committee, held hearings on it in mid-2011, and then let it sit there until the Congress ended in January 2013 without ever bringing it to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2011, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The committee held hearings on the legislation on June 23 and July 20, 2011, printed as S.Hrg. 112-220.
No further action was taken after the July 2011 hearings: the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still in committee.
The bill had 31 cosponsors, nearly all Republicans, giving it no realistic path to the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome a Senate filibuster even if it had been brought up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing regulatory system and the public protections it enforces are intact; agencies can still issue major rules without congressional approval, and businesses affected by those rules did not get the new veto they sought.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the REINS Act and assembled 31 cosponsors for it

for.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in June and July 2011 but took no further action and never voted on it

sides.party_line_note: All 30 Republican cosponsors plus one Democrat signed on; with only one Democrat in support, the bill had no path through a Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.note: Major rules on pollution, workplace safety, and consumer protection could be blocked by a single chamber's inaction, sharply reducing compliance costs. For ordinary people this means weaker enforcement of clean air, safe products, and fair markets.

Agencies would lose the ability to put major rules into effect on their own authority, making their statutory mandates much harder to carry out. Congress, not experts, would become the final gatekeeper.
Members would gain power over policy detail but also assume on-the-record votes on every contentious rule, a political cost most were unwilling to take on during this Congress.
